newsitem.title: USA: Growth,jobs,low inflation may coexist - Atlanta Fed.
newsitem.headline: Growth,jobs,low inflation may coexist - Atlanta Fed.

text.p: In a challenge to long established economic theories, low U.S. inflation may be able to coexist with healthy growth and low unemployment, Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta president Jack Guynn said on Friday.
"There is the possibility that we can have low inflation and low unemployment and strong growth," Guynn told Reuters.
Guynn, a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), said he was personally considering such a possibility, based on the recent performance of the U.S. economy.
The policy-setting FOMC next meets on August 19.

Guynn, who spoke to Reuters after addressing the Business Development Board of Palm Beach County, pointed out that the performance of the U.S. economy in recent years "seems to fly in the face of the old notion that lower inflation can be achieved and maintained only with substantional sacrifices to employment and output growth."

Achieving and maintaining low inflation without a cost to output or job creation challenges economic theories based on the trade-off between price performance and the Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU).
It also challenges the theory known as opportunistic disinflation which suggests that, in the absence of tight credit, prices need an economic downturn to drift lower.
U.S. inflation, as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and other price gauges, has steadily fallen since the onset of the current expansion in April 1991.

In his speech, Guynn explained that the rate of inflation achieved by Fed policy was the key factor behind the success of the economy, since stable, low inflation removed major elements of uncertainity for business decisions and consumers.

Guynn also credited the solid U.S. expansion to the absence of major imbalances in the economy. In addition, he said that the corporate and consumer debt burden was in line with profits and income and that there were no leverage problems except for some sub-par borrowers.
However, Guynn said the jury is still out about whether the currently "quite good economy" results from temporary or structural changes.
"The question is whether this is transitory or permanent. We need time," Guynn said.
Fed chairman Alan Greenspan raised the same question in his recent testimony before Congress.
Guynn said "the pricing behavior is so very different" in this business cycle that it raised fundamental questions among policy makers and economists alike and warranted further studies and debate.
Guynn stressed the Fed will remain vigilant for signs of any "inflation creeping up."
Productivity gains also contributed to the healthy U.S. economy, Guynn said. Such gains are difficult to measure accurately in the service sector, he said.

The Atlanta Fed president said massive business investments in new technology have translated into increased corporate profits while the fall of trade barriers and increased deregulation have also contributed to the U.S. expansion.
Guynn also said he was satisfied with fiscal discipline, although he noted the problems with Social Security and Medicare have not been resolved.
